findings.claim: The board is named to students four times in lesson 1 (description, two places in the content, and the exam tip): "the Eduqas listening exam", "the Eduqas spec expects you to know".
findings.truth: House rule: this board is never named in student-facing text. Say "the listening exam" or "the specification".
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned strings; project rule feedback_eduqas_wjec_neutral_phrasing

findings.claim: Three board names in lesson 2: "the Eduqas GCSE Music listening exam", "the Eduqas set work Africa", "In the Eduqas listening exam".
findings.truth: Remove the board name; the exam and the set work can be named without it.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned strings

findings.claim: Five board names in lesson 3, including "The Eduqas spec requires you to identify..." and "The Eduqas spec covers several structural forms".
findings.truth: Use "the specification" and "the listening exam".
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned strings

findings.claim: "In the Eduqas GCSE Music listening exam, you need to identify chords..."
findings.truth: Use "the GCSE Music listening exam".
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned strings

findings.claim: Four board names in lesson 5, including the key-fact prompt "Recall the specific examples given for toto's “Africa” (the Eduqas set.", which is also cut off mid-sentence.
findings.truth: Remove the board name; the prompt is rewritten as a whole sentence.
findings.evidence: CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md banned strings

findings.claim: Question 2 ("State two differences between legato and staccato") is labelled "1 mark — Multiple Choice / One-word Answer" but its mark scheme awards up to 2 marks.
findings.truth: It is a 2-mark short-answer question. The label must match the scheme, because students judge answer length from the marks.
findings.evidence: recomputation of the question's own mark scheme

findings.claim: Question 6 mark scheme says "level-based marking, QWC assessed".
findings.truth: Written communication carries no separate marks in this exam. The appraising paper is 96 marks split across AO3 (20%) and AO4 (20%); no SPaG or QWC allocation exists.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1 assessment objectives and weightings; spec 2.3 Component 3

findings.claim: Question 6 is labelled "12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)" but asks a single general discussion question with no extract and no score.
findings.truth: It is an extended listening response. Only the two prepared extracts (the study piece for forms and devices, and Africa) come with printed score sections.
findings.evidence: spec, Assessment of Component 3 (scores printed only where a question needs them)

findings.claim: Flashcard 4 answer is "1600ndash1750" for the question "_____ dynamics tend to change suddenly between loud and quiet sections".
findings.truth: The answer text is a mangled entity and does not answer the question. The card is rebuilt: "In _____ music (about 1600 to 1750), dynamics tend to change suddenly..." → Baroque.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own text; standard period dates (Baroque c.1600–1750)

findings.claim: Flashcard 5 answer is "1820ndash1900" for the question "_____ composers used a much wider range of dynamics...".
findings.truth: Same fault. Rebuilt as "In _____ music (about 1820 to 1900), composers used a much wider range of dynamics..." → Romantic.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own text; standard period dates (Romantic c.1820–1900)

findings.claim: "In an exam question on the musical Blood Brothers, the accepted answers for a slow tempo were Adagio, Lento or Largo."
findings.truth: A past-paper question and its accepted answers must not appear. The teaching point survives without it: for a slow extract, Adagio, Lento or Largo are all accepted.
findings.evidence: house copyright-distancing rule in CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md

findings.claim: "In 3/4 the stress is 1-2-3, while in 6/8 the stress is 1-2-3-4-5-6 with two main pulses."
findings.truth: 6/8 does not stress all six quavers. It has two dotted-crotchet beats, so the stresses fall on 1 and 4. This is exactly the distinction a listening question asks for.
findings.evidence: standard theory; spec Appendix C lists compound time 6/8, 9/8, 12/8

findings.claim: Question 2 is labelled 4 marks but its scheme caps at 2; question 3 is labelled 4 marks but its scheme caps at 3.
findings.truth: Labels corrected to 2 and 3 marks to match the schemes.
findings.evidence: recomputation of each question's mark scheme

findings.claim: Two schemes open with the rubric phrase "Award up to N marks for:".
findings.truth: House wording is "Up to N marks:".
findings.evidence: house copyright-distancing rule (banned rubric phrases)

findings.claim: Question 5 carries a full set of board-style level descriptors ("9–10: Perceptive answer... 0: No valid information") under the heading "Level descriptors".
findings.truth: Board level wording must not be pasted in. Replaced with the house band names (Top / Upper-mid / Mid / Lower-mid / Low band) in our own words.
findings.evidence: house copyright-distancing rule in CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md

findings.claim: A key-fact prompt reads "Can you name all 2 main textures from memory?" above a box that names four textures.
findings.truth: Four: monophonic, homophonic, polyphonic and unison.
findings.evidence: the same key-fact box; spec Appendix C texture list

findings.claim: Question 2 ("State two ways in which the texture of Verse 2 differs from Verse 1") is labelled "1 mark — Multiple Choice / One-word Answer" but its scheme gives 2 marks.
findings.truth: It is a 2-mark short-answer question.
findings.evidence: recomputation of the question's own mark scheme

findings.claim: Flashcard 4 repeats the answer of flashcard 1 ("Harmony") with a cloze copy of the opening sentence.
findings.truth: Two cards in one lesson must not share an answer. Replaced with Modulation, a term the lesson defines.
findings.evidence: validator limit in CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC.md; lesson glossary

findings.claim: Flashcard 5 answer is "Generated" and its question is "_____ diagram for Harmony and Tonality The rate at which chords change is called the harmonic rhythm" — built from an image caption.
findings.truth: The card is meaningless. Replaced with Perfect cadence (V → I), taught in the same lesson.
findings.evidence: the lesson's cadence section

findings.claim: Question 6 ends "[Quality of written communication will be assessed in this question.]"
findings.truth: No separate written-communication marks exist in this exam (AO3 20% + AO4 20% = the whole 96-mark paper).
findings.evidence: spec 3.1 assessment objectives and weightings

findings.claim: "Note the use of chord inversions (B/F#, A/E, E/F#) to create a smooth bass line" — repeated in the question 4 answer key.
findings.truth: E/F# is not an inversion. The E chord is E–G#–B, so F# is not one of its notes; it is a slash chord over a non-chord bass. B/F# (Ic) and A/E are genuine inversions.
findings.evidence: triad spelling of E major; standard inversion definition

findings.claim: Question 2 is labelled 4 marks but its scheme caps at 2; question 3 is labelled 4 marks but its scheme caps at 3.
findings.truth: Labels corrected to 2 and 3 marks.
findings.evidence: recomputation of each question's mark scheme

findings.claim: "The xylophones and marimbas that follow have a bright, resonant, bell-like sonority..."
findings.truth: No tuned percussion plays the riff. Jeff Porcaro programmed the kalimba-style riff on a Yamaha GS-1 and layered six takes; the sounds only imitate African tuned percussion. The lesson's own instrument list already says synthesiser, and the key fact says the sonorities "suggest" those instruments.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Africa (Toto song) — recording section

findings.claim: Question 3 asks for "three ways" but is labelled 4 marks and its scheme gives 1 mark a point up to 4.
findings.truth: Question reworded to ask for four ways; the scheme lists five possible points.
findings.evidence: recomputation of the question's own mark scheme

findings.claim: The verse harmony is given as a "9-bar chord sequence" but ten chords are listed (B–D#m7–G#m7–B/F#–A/E–E/F#–G#m7–A–G#m7–C#m), while the harmonic rhythm is stated as one chord per bar.
findings.truth: Three readings are possible: the sequence spans ten bars; one bar carries two chords; or the ninth bar is the silent bar named in lesson 1 and the tenth chord starts the next phrase. The score settles it. Nothing is edited until it is checked.
findings.evidence: internal arithmetic across lessons 1, 3 and 4

findings.claim: Lesson 1 says the instrumental melody at bars 66–69 uses a B major pentatonic scale; lessons 3 and 4 say Riff B — on which the instrumental melody is based — uses the E major pentatonic.
findings.truth: Both can be true if the two halves differ (lesson 1 also says bars 70–74 move to E). Worth one check against the score when lesson 4 is adjudicated.
findings.evidence: cross-reading of lessons 1, 3 and 4

findings.claim: Lesson 2 groups Vivace with Presto as "very fast".
findings.truth: The specification's term list pairs Allegro/Vivace. Either grouping earns the mark, and the lesson's answer key accepts Allegro, Vivace and Presto for a fast extract, so no edit.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix C, Tempo list

findings.claim: Lesson 4 teaches chord vii° as a secondary chord.
findings.truth: The musical language section requires roman numerals for I, ii, iii, IV, V and vi only. Teaching vii° is extra, not wrong.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3, Musical Language

findings.claim: "In recorded rock and pop music, panning is used most commonly on the drum kit."
findings.truth: A production generalisation with no source. Harmless, but it is not a fact a student should quote as a rule.
findings.evidence: no source found

findings.claim: Electric guitar and bass guitar are listed as "electronic instruments".
findings.truth: They are electric (amplified pickups) rather than electronic (sound generated by circuits). The shorthand is common at GCSE and the lesson explains the amplification point, so no edit.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix C lists them under Sonority, with Synthesised/electronic kept for Technology

summary: All five lessons name the exam board to students (17 places) and all five carry practice questions whose mark label contradicts their own mark scheme. The hard content errors are four broken auto-generated flashcards (two mangled entities in lesson 2, a duplicate answer and a card built from an image caption in lesson 4), two false claims that written communication is separately marked, a 6/8 stress statement that would lose a metre mark, E/F# taught as a chord inversion, and Africa's synthesised riff described as real xylophones and marimbas. Music theory, cadences, Italian terms, note values and every knowledge-check answer key checked clean.
